explanations.explanation: Yep, that's what the Teacher saw: "A righteous man perishing in his righteousness." (Ecclesiastes 7:15) It's not what you'd expect, and he says so right out loud. I think that's why he calls his life futile before he even says it. Sometimes the Bible just tells you the hard part plainly.

explanations.answer: He lives long in his righteousness
explanations.explanation: That's the twist, friend. The Teacher says the long life went to the other guy: "a wicked man living long in his wickedness." (Ecclesiastes 7:15) The righteous man is the one he saw perishing. It's the kind of thing that makes you set your spatula down and stare at the wall.

explanations.answer: He is honored by every king
explanations.explanation: No kings show up in this verse at all. The Teacher just says he saw "A righteous man perishing in his righteousness." (Ecclesiastes 7:15) No parade, no medals, nothing. Honestly, that's the whole shock of it.

Close, but the Teacher says it the other way around. He saw "a wicked man living long in his wickedness." (Ecclesiastes 7:15) Long, not young. That's the part that makes you go, hold on, say that again?

Right, no early funeral for the wicked man here. The text says he saw "a wicked man living long in his wickedness." (Ecclesiastes 7:15) The righteous man is the one perishing. Two things that don't match up, and the Teacher just says it straight.

That's it. "Do not be overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself?" (Ecclesiastes 7:16) The Teacher is asking a real question there. I'll be honest, I read that and my hat tilted a little.

It's actually true, and I know, it sounds odd. The Teacher says, "Do not be overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself?" (Ecclesiastes 7:16) He's warning about going too far. The text puts it in his own words, so we leave it just like that.

explanations.answer: You could die before your time
explanations.explanation: You've got it. "Why should you die before your time?" (Ecclesiastes 7:17) That's the question the Teacher asks about being excessively wicked or a fool. He doesn't sugarcoat it, and neither will I.
Money never comes up in this verse, friend. The Teacher asks, "Why should you die before your time?" (Ecclesiastes 7:17) That's the danger he names. Nothing about a will or a bank account.

explanations.answer: You could be driven from the city
explanations.explanation: Nobody gets run out of town here. The Teacher asks, "Why should you die before your time?" (Ecclesiastes 7:17) That's the warning for being excessively wicked or a fool. Short and serious.
Yes, ma'am, yes, sir! "For he who fears God will follow both warnings." (Ecclesiastes 7:18) The Teacher puts it right there at the end of the verse. Fearing God is where he lands.
Money doesn't get a seat at this table. The Teacher says, "For he who fears God will follow both warnings." (Ecclesiastes 7:18) That's the one who follows them. Not the one counting coins.
I hear you, but the text points somewhere else. "For he who fears God will follow both warnings." (Ecclesiastes 7:18) Fearing God is what the Teacher names. Trusting yourself isn't in the verse.

That's right. "Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins." (Ecclesiastes 7:20) The Teacher says it about everybody. And yes, that includes the guy who always shows up with the perfect casserole. Wait, wrong food. The guy with the perfect cookies, I mean me.

It's true, friend, and the Teacher doesn't leave any wiggle room. "Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins." (Ecclesiastes 7:20) Nobody on earth is in the exception pile. That's a lot of us in the same boat, and I'm sitting in it with you.

Right on target. The Teacher says, "or you may hear your servant cursing you." (Ecclesiastes 7:21) That's what you might overhear. Listening to every word is a good way to ruin a perfectly fine afternoon.

Wouldn't that be nice? The Teacher says something else: "or you may hear your servant cursing you." (Ecclesiastes 7:21) So the word is cursing. Nobody ever overhears a compliment and then regrets listening.
I wish, friend! A thank you would've made this a short verse. The Teacher says, "or you may hear your servant cursing you." (Ecclesiastes 7:21) That's why he says not to listen to every word.

explanations.answer: You have cursed others many times yourself
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. "For you know in your heart that many times you yourself have cursed others." (Ecclesiastes 7:22) The Teacher is saying you know this from your own heart. Gentle, but it lands.

explanations.answer: Servants are never pleased with anyone
explanations.explanation: The Teacher doesn't say anything like that about servants. His reason turns the mirror around: "For you know in your heart that many times you yourself have cursed others." (Ecclesiastes 7:22) It's about what you know about yourself. I felt that one in my apron.

explanations.answer: Curses can never harm a wise man
explanations.explanation: That's not in the text. The Teacher gives a different reason: "For you know in your heart that many times you yourself have cursed others." (Ecclesiastes 7:22) He points back at your own heart. Not at how tough a wise man is.
Yes, that's how he says it. "I resolve to be wise." But it was beyond me." (Ecclesiastes 7:23) He tested everything by wisdom, and it still outran him. I think that's a humble thing to admit.

explanations.answer: He found every answer he sought
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The Teacher says he resolved to be wise, "But it was beyond me." (Ecclesiastes 7:23) So there were answers he didn't find. He says that out loud and doesn't hide it.

explanations.answer: He was praised throughout the city
explanations.explanation: No crowds cheering in this verse. The Teacher says he resolved to be wise, "But it was beyond me." (Ecclesiastes 7:23) That's the whole result. A quiet, honest line.
That's right. "What exists is out of reach and very deep. Who can fathom it?" (Ecclesiastes 7:24) The Teacher says it plainly. Out of reach and very deep, and then he asks the question.
It's true, friend. The Teacher says, "What exists is out of reach and very deep. Who can fathom it?" (Ecclesiastes 7:24) He's not saying everything is simple. He's saying it's deep and hard to reach.

explanations.answer: The stupidity of wickedness and the folly of madness
explanations.explanation: Yep, that's the list. He says he directed his mind "to understand the stupidity of wickedness and the folly of madness." (Ecclesiastes 7:25) It sits right beside wisdom and explanations. That's some serious homework.

explanations.answer: The paths of the stars and the depths of the sea
explanations.explanation: Pretty, but it's not in the verse. The Teacher says he set his mind "to understand the stupidity of wickedness and the folly of madness." (Ecclesiastes 7:25) No stars, no sea. Even though I do love a good sky.

explanations.answer: The riches of kings and the strength of armies
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. The Teacher says he set his mind "to understand the stupidity of wickedness and the folly of madness." (Ecclesiastes 7:25) Kings and armies don't make the list. This one's about wickedness and folly.
You got it. "The man who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is ensnared." (Ecclesiastes 7:26) The Teacher puts those two side by side. Pleasing God is the one who gets away.
Strength isn't what the Teacher names. He says, "The man who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is ensnared." (Ecclesiastes 7:26) Nothing about muscles. Not even mustache muscles.
A fat wallet isn't the answer here. The Teacher says, "The man who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is ensnared." (Ecclesiastes 7:26) That's who escapes. Riches never come up.
That's the word. "While my soul was still searching but not finding." (Ecclesiastes 7:28) He kept looking even when he wasn't finding. I know a little about that, I once searched a drawer for years.
No naps for the Teacher here. He says, "While my soul was still searching but not finding." (Ecclesiastes 7:28) His soul kept at it. Searching, not resting.
Not yet, friend. The Teacher says, "While my soul was still searching but not finding." (Ecclesiastes 7:28) He's still looking, and nothing's turned up. No confetti at this point.
Right on the money. "God made mankind upright, but they have sought out many schemes." (Ecclesiastes 7:29) That's what the Teacher says he found. One thing, and it's about all of us.

explanations.answer: They were led astray by kings
explanations.explanation: Kings aren't blamed in this verse. The Teacher says, "God made mankind upright, but they have sought out many schemes." (Ecclesiastes 7:29) The schemes were what mankind sought out. That's the line as he gives it.

explanations.answer: They grew tired of doing good
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say tired. The Teacher says, "God made mankind upright, but they have sought out many schemes." (Ecclesiastes 7:29) The word is schemes, and there were many. So that's the answer.
